title: Turning the other cheek in the old Scripture
source_text: Ὁ μὲν οὖν Κέλσος, μὴ ἀντιπαραθεὶς τὰ δοκοῦντα ἐναντία ἀπὸ τοῦ νόμου τοῖς ἀπὸ τοῦ εὐαγγελίου, φησὶ καὶ τό· τῷ δ᾿ ἅπαξ τυπτήσαντι παρέχειν καὶ αὖθις τύπτειν. ἡμεῖς δ᾿ ἐροῦμεν εἰδέναι μὲν καὶ τὸ „ὀφθαλμὸν ἀντὶ ὀφθαλμοῦ καὶ ὀδόντα ἀντὶ ὀδόντος“ εἰρημένον τοῖς πάλαι ἀνεγνωκέναι δὲ καὶ τὸ „ἐγὼ δὲ λέγω ὑμῖν“· „τῷ τύπτοντί σε εἰς τὴν σιαγόνα πάρεχε καὶ τὴν ἄλλην.“ ἀλλ᾿ ἐπεὶ περιηχηθεὶς οἶμαι ὁ Κέλσος ἀπὸ τῶν διαιρούντων τὴν κατὰ τὸ εὐαγγέλιον θεότητα ἐκ τῆς νομικῆς θεότητος τὰ τοιαῦτα τίθησι, λεκτέον πρὸς τὸν λόγον αὐτοῦ ὅτι οἶδε καὶ τὰ παλαιὰ γράμματα (τὸ) „τῷ τύπτοντί σε εἰς τὴν δεξιὰν σιαγόνα πάρεχε καὶ τὴν ἄλλην.“ ἐν γοῦν τοῖς Ἱερεμίου Θρήνοις γέγραπται· „ἀγαθὸν ἀνδρὶ, ὅταν ἄρῃ ζυγὸν ἐν νεότητι αὐτοῦ, καθήσεται κατὰ μόνας καὶ σιωπήσεται, ὅτι ἦρεν ἐφ᾿ ἑαυτῷ. δώσει τῷ παίοντι αὐτὸν σιαγόνα, καὶ χορτασθήσεται ὀνειδισμῶν.“ οὐκ ἀντιδιατάσσεται θεοῦ τὸ εὐαγγέλιον τῷ τοῦ νόμου θεῷ οὐδὲ περὶ τῆς κατὰ τὸ ῥητὸν κατὰ κόῤῥης πληγῆς· οὐδ᾿ ὁπότερος ψεύδεται, οὔτε Μωϋσῆς οὔτε Ἰησοῦς, οὐδ᾿ ὁ πατὴρ τὸν Ἰησοῦν πέμπων ἐπελάθετο, τίνα Μωϋσεῖ διετάξατο· ἀλλ᾿ οὐδὲ καταγνοὺς τῶν ἰδίων νόμων μετέγνω καὶ τὸν ἄγγελον ἐπὶ τοῖς ἐναντίοις ἀποστέλλει.
pass_a_gloss: Celsus, then, not setting against-alongside (ἀντιπαρατίθημι) the things seeming (δοκέω) contrary from the law to those from the gospel, says also this: to offer (παρέχω) to the one who struck (τύπτω) once (ἅπαξ) to strike again (αὖθις). But we shall say that we know (οἶδα) also 'eye (ὀφθαλμός) for eye and tooth (ὀδούς) for tooth' said to those of old (οἱ πάλαι), and have read (ἀναγιγνώσκω) also 'but I say to you': 'to the one striking you on the cheek (σιαγών) offer also the other.' But since, I think (οἶμαι), Celsus, having been dinned round (περιηχέω) by those dividing (διαιρέω) the deity (θεότης) according to the gospel from the legal (νομικός) deity, sets such things down, one must say to his argument (λόγος) that the old writings (παλαιὰ γράμματα) also know 'to the one striking you on the right (δεξιός) cheek offer also the other.' At any rate in the Lamentations (Θρῆνοι) of Jeremiah it is written: 'Good for a man (ἀνήρ), when he lifts (αἴρω) a yoke (ζυγός) in his youth (νεότης); he will sit alone (κατὰ μόνας) and be silent (σιωπάω), because he lifted it upon himself. He will give to the one smiting (παίω) him a cheek, and will be filled (χορτάζω) with reproaches (ὀνειδισμοί).' The gospel of God does not counter-order (ἀντιδιατάσσομαι) to the God of the law, not even about the blow (πληγή) on the cheek/temple (κατὰ κόρρης) according to the letter (ῥητόν); nor does either (ὁπότερος) lie (ψεύδομαι), neither Moses nor Jesus, nor did the Father sending Jesus forget (ἐπιλανθάνομαι) what he ordered (διατάσσω) Moses; but neither, having condemned (καταγιγνώσκω) his own laws, did he repent (μεταγιγνώσκω) and send (ἀποστέλλω) the messenger/angel (ἄγγελος) for the opposite things.
pass_b_english: Celsus, then, without setting the passages from the Law that seem contrary beside those from the Gospel, also says this: “to let the man who has struck once strike again.” We shall reply that we know the saying “An eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth,” spoken to the men of old (Matthew 5:38; Exodus 21:24), and that we have also read “But I say to you” (Matthew 5:39): “To the one who strikes you on the cheek, offer the other also” (Luke 6:29).

But since Celsus, I think, has had his ears filled by those who divide the deity of the Gospel from the deity of the Law, and so puts forward such things, we must say in answer to his argument that the old writings too know the saying “To the one who strikes you on the right cheek, offer the other also” (Matthew 5:39). At any rate, it is written in the Lamentations of Jeremiah: “It is good for a man when he bears a yoke in his youth. He will sit alone and keep silent, because he has taken it upon himself. He will give his cheek to the one who strikes him, and he will be filled with reproaches” (Lamentations 3:27–28, 30).

The Gospel of God does not issue orders contrary to the God of the Law, not even about the blow on the cheek taken literally. Neither of the two is lying, neither Moses nor Jesus; nor did the Father, in sending Jesus, forget what he had commanded Moses; nor indeed did he condemn his own laws, change his mind, and send his messenger for the opposite purpose.

choices.choice: Celsus’s words (from 7.18) are given in double quotation marks: τῷ δ᾿ ἅπαξ τυπτήσαντι παρέχειν καὶ αὖθις τύπτειν, ‘to let the man who has struck once strike again’. ‘An eye for an eye’ is quoted from the Law (Exodus 21:24; also Leviticus 24:20; Deuteronomy 19:21) as Jesus cites it in Matthew 5:38; τοῖς πάλαι echoes Matthew’s ‘it was said to those of old’. The first cheek saying follows Luke 6:29 (τῷ τύπτοντί σε ἐπὶ τὴν σιαγόνα πάρεχε καὶ τὴν ἄλλην; Origen has εἰς); the second, with ‘right’, is Matthew 5:39 in substance (Matthew has ὅστις σε ῥαπίζει ... στρέψον). The critics who ‘divide the deity of the Gospel from the deity of the Law’ are evidently the Marcionites, but Origen does not name them here. The Lamentations quotation is Septuagint Lamentations 3:27–28 and 3:30, skipping verse 29; English numbering is the same. οὐκ ἀντιδιατάσσεται θεοῦ τὸ εὐαγγέλιον τῷ τοῦ νόμου θεῷ is translated as printed (‘The Gospel of God’); the sense may be ‘the God of the Gospel’. κατὰ κόρρης (‘on the temple, a slap on the face’) is rendered ‘on the cheek’ to match the sayings. The last sentence answers Celsus’s questions in 7.18 point by point, using his words (ψεύδεται, ἐπελάθετο, καταγνοὺς ... μετέγνω, τὸν ἄγγελον); ἄγγελος is rendered ‘messenger’, as in Celsus’s question, meaning Jesus. Origen does not mark these as a quotation, so no quotation marks are used.
'also cites this saying' changed to 'also says this' (φησί; the words are Celsus's own paraphrase, not a cited text)
'the precept' changed to 'the saying' (Greek has only the article τό)
Checked Matthew 5:38-39, Exodus 21:24, Luke 6:29, Lamentations 3:27-28, 30 LXX; speaker attributions (Celsus, Origen's 'I think') correct
